w: Inhabited since the Neolithic, this hilltop became capital of the Kingdom of Ammon, then passed through Assyrian, Roman, and Byzantine hands before the Umayyads built a palace on it -- abandoned for centuries until Circassian refugees resettled it in 1878. The Temple of Hercules' columns still crown the skyline.
_facts: among the world's oldest continuously inhabited places, evidence since the Neolithic, fortified in the Bronze Age (1800 BCE)
became capital of the Kingdom of Ammon after 1200 BCE, later under Assyrian, Babylonian, Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad empires
major remains are the Temple of Hercules, a Byzantine church, and the Umayyad Palace
abandoned after the Umayyads for much of a millennium until Ottoman-era Circassian refugees resettled it in 1878; Jordan Archaeological Museum built on the hill in 1951

w: Named for the king who commissioned it, this is Jordan's largest mosque -- and, unusually, a religious museum sharing the very same building, the Prophet Muhammad Museum folded into the same complex, prayer hall and exhibits under one roof in the capital.
s: Jordan's biggest mosque, doubling as a museum
_facts: the King Hussein Bin Talal Mosque is a mosque and religious museum in Amman
it is the largest mosque in Jordan

w: Egypt's Coptic Orthodox Church planted this one directly in front of the King Abdullah I Mosque's blue dome, timed to Pope Shenouda III's 2005 visit to Jordan -- a small outpost of Alexandria's Christianity, facing off against Amman's grandest minarets.
s: A Coptic church facing the Blue Dome mosque
_facts: Virgin Mary Coptic Orthodox Church, lies in front of the King Abdullah I Mosque in the Abdali district
built during Pope Shenouda III of Alexandria's visit to Jordan in 2005

w: King Hussein inaugurated this memorial himself in 1977, dedicating it to Jordanians who died in service since 1915 -- starting with the Great Arab Revolt his own great-grandfather led. Inside sit the weapons, uniforms, and vehicles of a century of Jordanian military history. Entry is free, for anyone, no exceptions.
s: A war museum King Hussein opened himself
_facts: established on King Hussein's wishes, inaugurated by him on 25 July 1977, located next to Amman Sport City
showcases Jordan's military weapons, clothing and vehicles
memorial to martyrs who served Jordan as early as 1915, starting with the Great Arab Revolt led by Hussein bin Ali
about 70,000 visitors a year, entry free for all regardless of nationality

w: Also called the Latin Church of Jabal Amman, this Catholic parish turned itself into a shelter in 2015, housing Iraqi refugees after King Abdullah II invited Iraq's Christians to Jordan -- one of more than forty churches nationwide that took families in, with Vatican-approved funding behind it.
s: A church that became a refugee shelter
_facts: also called the Latin Church of Jabal Amman, dedicated to Joseph of Nazareth, under the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem
in 2015 housed refugees who fled the war in Iraq
one of more than 40 churches adopted after King Abdullah II invited Iraqi Christians to Jordan, with Vatican funds approved

w: Wedged beside the Roman amphitheater downtown, this 1971 museum sorts Jordanian folk culture into three baskets -- desert Bedu, village Reef, and town Madineh -- through costumes, instruments, and handicrafts, plus a scatter of ancient mosaics for good measure.
s: Jordan's folk culture, sorted three ways
_facts: located next to the Roman amphitheater, established 1971
showcases Jordanian cultural heritage items from the desert (Bedu), villages (Reef), and towns (Madineh)
includes costumes, musical instruments, handicrafts and mosaics

w: This squat stone tower dates to the Iron Age Ammonite Kingdom, rebuilt and reused by the Romans centuries later. Archaeologist Nelson Glueck once read it as a border fort guarding the kingdom's edge; more recent research suggests a farm or home instead. Its twin to the south is gone entirely.
s: An Iron Age tower, reused by Rome
_facts: round stone tower and storerooms on the northern side of Jabal Amman, possibly built mid-1st millennium BCE (Iron Age II, Ammonite Kingdom)
rebuilt and reused during the Roman period
Nelson Glueck interpreted such towers in 1939 as Ammonite border forts; more recent views suggest agricultural or residential use
a smaller southern twin tower is now destroyed

w: Under its blue mosaic dome, 3,000 worshippers can pray at once -- and tourists are welcome too, provided they cover up; a free hooded gown waits at the door for anyone who shows up bare-armed. Built between 1982 and 1989 and named for the king who founded modern Jordan.
_facts: built 1982-1989, capped by a blue mosaic dome beneath which 3,000 Muslims may pray, in the Abdali area
tourists allowed to visit; dress code enforced with a free hooded gown provided

w: Built as an Umayyad mosque in the 7th century over an older Byzantine basilica, this one has been torn down and rebuilt more than once -- most recently in 1924 on King Abdullah I's orders, renamed for his father Sharif Hussein. It has remained downtown Amman's default gathering point for political protest ever since.
s: Amman's mosque, and its default protest square
_facts: built as an Omari Mosque in the 7th century CE under Umar Bin El Khattab, on the site of an older Byzantine basilica
original mosque demolished by orders of Abdullah I in 1924, rebuilt and renamed for his father Sharif Hussein bin Ali
one of the first new buildings after the 1921 establishment of the Emirate of Transjordan
a gathering point for political demonstrations in Amman

n: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
w: Inaugurated in 1980 under King Hussein and Queen Noor's patronage, this gallery built a collection few expect in Amman -- over 2,000 works from more than 800 artists across 59 countries, weighted toward Asia and Africa rather than the usual European canon.
_facts: inaugurated 1980 under patronage of King Hussein and Queen Noor, established by the Royal Society of Fine Arts
permanent collection of over 2,000 works by more than 800 artists from 59 countries, mainly Asia and Africa
_sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts

w: Around 110 tanks and armored vehicles sit in strict chronological order across this museum's grounds -- American, British, Soviet, and German steel tracing a century of warfare since 1915. It took nearly ten years to build, and still runs live demonstrations of tanks rolling through an outdoor arena.
_facts: inaugurated 29 January 2018, next to King Abdullah II Park in Al Muqabalain, spans about 20,000 square meters
houses around 110 tanks and armored vehicles from Jordan, Arab nations and foreign countries, in chronological order since 1915
took nearly ten years to construct, designed by Jordanian architect Zaid Daoud
features a demonstration program in an outdoor arena

w: Workers digging a drainage system in 2020 hit Roman baths nobody knew were there, along with two statues and pottery spanning four empires -- Roman, Byzantine, Umayyad, Ottoman. With no funds to excavate, the site was reburied in silica sand for some future dig. Downtown Amman may be sitting on more.
s: Roman baths, found by accident, reburied on purpose
_facts: uncovered in downtown Amman in 2020 during infrastructure works for an underground drainage system
two Roman statues found, plus ceramics from Roman, Byzantine, Umayyad, and Ottoman eras
reburied using high-silica sand for future excavation due to lack of funds
speculation that more ancient ruins lie beneath downtown Amman

w: The legend goes that seven young men hid here around 250 AD, fleeing Roman emperor Decius's persecution, and woke up centuries later -- a story told in both Christian and Quranic tradition as the Sleepers of Ephesus and the Companions of the Cave. Rediscovered in 1951; several other caves claim the same story.
s: The cave where seven sleepers reputedly woke
_facts: archaeological and religious site in ar-Rajib village east of Amman
claimed to have housed the Seven Sleepers, known in Christian sources as Sleepers of Ephesus and in the Quran as Companions of the Cave
legend says the men fled Roman emperor Decius's persecution around AD 250 and emerged centuries later
rediscovered in 1951; one of several caves associated with the legend

w: Seat of the Melkite Greek Catholic Archeparchy of Petra and Philadelphia -- a title reaching back to Amman's old Greek name -- this cathedral hosted Pope Benedict XVI in 2009, one of the Vatican's highest-profile visits to the city in decades.
s: A cathedral named for old Roman Amman
_facts: Greek-Melkite Cathedral of St. George, headquarters of the Melkite Greek Catholic Archeparchy of Petra and Philadelphia, created 1932 by Pope Pius XI's bull
Pope Benedict XVI visited on 9 May 2009
